question: Which statement best describes Typing props?
options: DOM handlers receive React's synthetic event types parameterized by the element, so fields like e.target.value are correctly typed. Use React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement> for inputs, React.MouseEvent for clicks, and React.FormEvent for form submits. Getting the element generic right is what makes e.target.value a string instead of any.

Hooks are generic functions whose type argument tells the compiler what value they hold. useState infers from the initial value but needs an explicit generic when the eventual type is broader — useState(null) infers null and useState([]) infers never[]. useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null) types a DOM ref whose .current is T | null and must be guarded.

Props are the public API of a component, so you describe their exact shape with an interface or type and annotate the parameter directly: function Button(props: ButtonProps). The compiler then verifies every <Button /> call site — flagging missing required props, misspellings, and wrong types before the code runs. Prefer this over React.FC, which adds an implicit children prop and complicates generics.

When a component wraps arbitrary content, type its children as React.ReactNode — the broadest renderable type, covering JSX, strings, numbers, arrays, fragments, and null. Avoid the narrower JSX.Element (rejects strings/arrays) or React.ReactElement. This is the idiomatic way to type layout, card, and provider components.

A generic component works for any item type while keeping callbacks fully typed. You declare a type parameter <T,> and TypeScript infers T from the props at each call site, so a renderItem callback receives a precisely-typed item. A discriminated (tagged) union models mutually exclusive prop combinations using a shared literal field. It expresses 'these props are required together' in a way a flat interface with optional fields cannot — making invalid states unrepresentable rather than caught at runtime. TypeScript narrows the union by the discriminant inside the component and at the call site.

Mark optional props with ? and supply defaults in the destructure rather than scattering undefined checks through the body. question: Which statement best describes Generic components?
options: any disables type checking for a value and silently spreads through your code, defeating the point of TypeScript. Prefer unknown for untrusted input, which forces a narrowing check before use, and validate external data (fetch responses) with a schema before trusting its type. A type assertion (as User) lies to the compiler and gives no runtime guarantee — never assert past untrusted input.
